description: 45 gym and fitness logos with names, explained by a brand designer: big chains like Planet Fitness, LA Fitness, and Crunch, premium clubs like Life Time and Equinox, and boutique studios.
intro:
A gym logo has to work on a giant building sign, a key fob, a t-shirt, and an app icon, and it has to tell people in a second what kind of gym it is: cheap and friendly, hardcore, or luxury. The best gym logos are bold, simple, and full of energy, and they match the price point and the people they want to attract.

What makes a good gym logo?

A clear price signal: budget gyms like Planet Fitness and Basic-Fit use bright colours and friendly type, while premium clubs like Equinox and Life Time use black, minimal wordmarks.

A symbol that works small: the Anytime Fitness running man, the Gold's Gym strongman, and the 24 Hour Fitness circle all work on key fobs, apparel, and apps.

Energy and movement: italic letters, swooshes, and bold weights make a logo feel fast and strong, which suits fitness.

Below are 45 gym and fitness logos with names, from big-box chains to premium clubs, budget gyms, boutique studios, and training franchises. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. For more ideas, see my guides to the logo design process, logo fonts, and logo colours.

logoResearch.name: Planet Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Planet Fitness was founded in Dover, New Hampshire, in 1992, and its clubs are branded as a "Judgement Free Zone".
observations: The PF badge works like a planet or a gear, so the initials become a friendly symbol.
Bold, rounded purple type makes the gym feel welcoming rather than intimidating.

logoResearch.name: LA Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: LA Fitness was founded in Los Angeles in 1984.
observations: A sharp swoosh above the name adds speed and energy.
Widely spaced capitals and a vertical bar split the name into "LA" and "Fitness".

logoResearch.name: Crunch Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Doug Levine started Crunch in a basement aerobics studio in New York City in 1989.
observations: Distressed, hand-drawn type gives the brand a rebellious, fun personality.
The clenched fist adds attitude, which matches the "No Judgments" slogan.

logoResearch.name: 24 Hour Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mark Mastrov co-founded the company in San Leandro, California, in 1983.
observations: The 24 inside a circle works as a compact icon and tells you the gym never closes.
Italic capitals lean forward, which suggests movement and speed.

logoResearch.name: Anytime Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Anytime Fitness was founded in Minnesota in 2002 as a 24/7 gym franchise.
observations: The running figure is drawn with a few bold strokes, so it reads instantly as movement.
The two words stack tightly, which makes the logo compact for signs and key fobs.

logoResearch.name: Gold's Gym
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Joe Gold opened the first Gold's Gym in Venice Beach, California, in 1965.
observations: The strongman lifting a barbell makes the logo instantly about bodybuilding.
The round yellow badge looks like a medal or a stamp of strength.

logoResearch.name: Snap Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Peter Taunton founded Snap Fitness in Minnesota in 2003.
observations: Lowercase red "snap" feels quick and energetic.
The small "24/7" next to the name highlights all-day access.

logoResearch.name: YMCA
logoResearch.verifiedFact: George Williams founded the YMCA in London in 1844, and the US organisation adopted "the Y" logo in 2010.
observations: The big Y, made of two angled shapes, is friendly and easy to recognise.
Lowercase "the" next to it reflects how people actually call it: the Y.

logoResearch.name: EōS Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: EōS Fitness is a high-value gym chain based in Phoenix, Arizona.
observations: Heavy italic capitals make the name feel fast and powerful.
A short tagline above the name, "Where There's a Will", adds motivation.

logoResearch.name: Life Time
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bahram Akradi founded Life Time in Minnesota in 1992, and the brand later dropped "Fitness" from its name.
observations: Tall, condensed capitals make the two short words strong and athletic.
Dropping "Fitness" positions the brand as a lifestyle, not just a gym.

logoResearch.name: Equinox
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Equinox opened its first club in New York City in 1991.
observations: Extremely wide letter spacing gives the name a luxury, fashion-brand feel.
The O is drawn in two halves, a single detail that makes the strict wordmark memorable.

logoResearch.name: Bay Club
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bay Club grew from the San Francisco Bay Club, which opened in 1977.
observations: The navy circle with stacked type looks like a club badge.
The friendly lettering keeps a premium club approachable.

logoResearch.name: Chelsea Piers Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Chelsea Piers opened as a sports complex on Manhattan's Hudson River piers in 1995.
observations: Tall, condensed capitals look like letters on a pier or a stadium.
The strong type suits a brand that covers sports, not just gyms.

logoResearch.name: David Lloyd Clubs
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Former tennis player David Lloyd opened his first club in Heston, London, in 1982.
observations: The founder's signature makes the logo personal and premium.
A small "Clubs" between two lines gives the signature structure.

logoResearch.name: Third Space
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Third Space opened its first club in London's Soho in 2001.
observations: Serif capitals make the gym look more like a private members' club.
Wide spacing adds a calm, luxury feel.

logoResearch.name: Virgin Active
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Richard Branson's Virgin Group launched Virgin Active in 1999.
observations: The red Virgin signature ties the gym to the wider Virgin brand family.
Lowercase "active" in grey keeps the gym name simple and friendly.

logoResearch.name: Fitness First
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Fitness First was founded in Bournemouth, England, in 1993.
observations: A flowing script joins the two words into one dynamic signature.
The two capital F's give the script a strong rhythm.

logoResearch.name: Holmes Place
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Holmes Place was founded in London in 1980 and runs premium clubs across Europe.
observations: An HP monogram in a circle works like a members' badge.
Thin, spaced capitals keep the logo elegant and calm.

logoResearch.name: Basic-Fit
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Basic-Fit is Europe's largest gym chain and is headquartered in the Netherlands.
observations: Bold orange capitals make the budget brand loud and easy to spot.
The hyphen and distressed letters add a sporty, energetic touch.

logoResearch.name: PureGym
logoResearch.verifiedFact: PureGym was founded in the UK in 2008 and bought the US chain Blink Fitness in 2024.
observations: A large P outline with a teal dot works as a simple app icon.
Bold capitals keep the low-cost brand clear and direct.

logoResearch.name: The Gym Group
logoResearch.verifiedFact: John Treharne founded The Gym Group in London in 2008.
observations: A lowercase g inside a circle works as a bold, playful icon.
Electric blue and lime green make the budget brand stand out on the high street.

logoResearch.name: Retro Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Eric Casaburi founded Retro Fitness in New Jersey in 2004.
observations: A bold retro script recalls 1970s and 80s sports logos.
The swoosh under the name adds speed and nostalgia.

logoResearch.name: VASA Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: VASA Fitness is a gym chain based in Utah.
observations: A big red V doubles as an icon and the first letter of the name.
Thin, spaced capitals contrast with the bold V.

logoResearch.name: Chuze Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Chuze Fitness is a family-owned gym chain founded in Southern California.
observations: White letters on a black block make the logo look like a bold sign.
The U with a dot adds a small, friendly detail to the name.

logoResearch.name: UFC Gym
logoResearch.verifiedFact: UFC Gym launched in 2009, bringing the mixed martial arts brand into fitness clubs.
observations: Heavy italic letters make the logo feel aggressive and fast, like the sport.
The underline ties UFC and GYM into one lockup.

logoResearch.name: Youfit
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Youfit is a budget gym chain based in Florida, known for its low monthly memberships.
observations: Rounded, chunky letters make the name feel friendly and approachable.
The word GYMS runs vertically beside the name, a compact detail that adds context.

logoResearch.name: Workout Anytime
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Workout Anytime is a 24-hour gym franchise based in Georgia.
observations: Heavy capitals make the name easy to read on a busy road.
A small 24 badge at the end reinforces round-the-clock access.

logoResearch.name: Orangetheory Fitness
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ellen Latham founded Orangetheory in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, in 2010.
observations: The orange O symbol looks like a burst of energy.
The name itself is the colour, which makes the brand easy to remember.

logoResearch.name: F45 Training
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rob Deutsch and Adam Gilchrist founded F45 in Sydney in 2013.
observations: Bold, outlined F45 letters with red and blue lines look like a sports team badge.
"Training" underneath keeps the focus on group workouts.

logoResearch.name: Barry's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Barry Jay opened the first Barry's Bootcamp in West Hollywood in 1998.
observations: Spaced, bold capitals make the short name confident.
Dropping "Bootcamp" from the logo made the brand simpler and more premium.

logoResearch.name: SoulCycle
logoResearch.verifiedFact: SoulCycle opened its first indoor cycling studio in New York City in 2006.
observations: A heavy sans serif makes the name punchy and modern.
The two words merge into one, like riders moving in sync.

logoResearch.name: Solidcore
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Anne Mahlum founded Solidcore in Washington, D.C., in 2013.
observations: Square brackets on a black block make a striking, minimal icon.
The brand writes its name in brackets too, as [solidcore].

logoResearch.name: CorePower Yoga
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Trevor Tice founded CorePower Yoga in Denver in 2002.
observations: The O is drawn like an eye or a target, which suggests focus.
Lowercase type and a yellow "yoga" keep the brand light and friendly.

logoResearch.name: Club Pilates
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Club Pilates was founded in San Diego in 2007.
observations: A flower-like mark between the words suggests balance and flow.
Thin, spaced capitals make the brand feel calm and refined.

logoResearch.name: Rumble
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rumble opened as a boxing-inspired fitness studio in New York City in 2017.
observations: The red drop shape looks like a boxing glove or a bead of sweat.
The name sits inside the shape, so the logo works as a single icon.

logoResearch.name: Pure Barre
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Carrie Rezabek Dorr founded Pure Barre in Detroit in 2001.
observations: A lowercase p in a circle works as a simple app icon.
Soft lowercase type in red feels feminine and energetic.

logoResearch.name: CrossFit
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Greg Glassman founded CrossFit in Santa Cruz, California, in 2000.
observations: Heavy, condensed letters look raw and powerful, like the workouts.
The two words are joined, which makes the name feel like one movement.

logoResearch.name: Les Mills
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Olympic athlete Les Mills opened his first gym in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1968.
observations: Custom, wide letters give the brand a distinctive, almost futuristic look.
The italic slant suggests the energy of its group workout programs.

logoResearch.name: 9Round
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Shannon Hudson founded 9Round in Greenville, South Carolina, in 2008.
observations: The 9 and R are combined into a compact red circle.
The name describes the workout: nine rounds of kickboxing training.

logoResearch.name: Burn Boot Camp
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Devan and Morgan Kline founded Burn Boot Camp in Huntersville, North Carolina, in 2012.
observations: Rounded, bold lowercase letters make the logo friendly and energetic.
The light blue colour feels fresh and approachable.

logoResearch.name: StretchLab
logoResearch.verifiedFact: StretchLab launched in Los Angeles in 2015 and is now part of Xponential Fitness.
observations: Condensed capitals for "Stretch" contrast with the coloured blocks behind "Lab".
The blocks look like a stretching scale or a colour chart.

logoResearch.name: Row House
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Row House began as a rowing studio in New York City and is now part of Xponential Fitness.
observations: The yellow W is drawn like two oars, a clever nod to rowing.
Bold capitals around it keep the logo strong and simple.

logoResearch.name: CycleBar
logoResearch.verifiedFact: CycleBar was founded in Cincinnati in 2004.
observations: The C is drawn like a wheel, linking the icon to indoor cycling.
Condensed italic letters lean forward, like a rider sprinting.

logoResearch.name: YogaSix
logoResearch.verifiedFact: YogaSix was founded in San Diego in 2012.
observations: The Y6 mark combines a letter and a number into one icon.
Wide capitals keep the name calm and clear.

logoResearch.name: Hotworx
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hotworx is a franchise of infrared sauna workout studios with 24-hour access.
observations: The O is drawn as a flame, which explains the heated workouts at a glance.
Heavy capitals and a descriptor line make the concept clear.

listIntro: The boards below show all 45 gym logos in one consistent format, grouped into big-box chains, premium clubs, budget gyms, boutique studios, and training franchises.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the gym's size, price, or workouts.
sectionIntroductions: The biggest gym chains need logos that read from the highway and on thousands of key fobs, so they use bold colour, strong symbols, and simple type.
Premium and luxury clubs behave like fashion or hotel brands, with black wordmarks, wide spacing, signatures, and badges.
Budget and mid-size gyms compete on price and energy, so their logos are loud, colourful, and built for busy high streets and strip malls.
Boutique studios sell one type of workout, and their logos are simple, punchy, and designed for Instagram and apparel.
Training and specialty franchises turn a method into a brand, with icons that explain the workout, from rowing oars to cycling wheels.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of gym and fitness logos, not a ranking of gyms.
Look at how each logo uses type, colour, and one symbol to signal its price point and personality.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a building sign, a key fob, and a t-shirt.

findings.heading: Price shows in the logo
findings.text: Budget gyms like Planet Fitness, Basic-Fit, and PureGym use bright colours and friendly type, while Equinox, Life Time, and Third Space use black, minimal wordmarks.

findings.heading: Symbols explain the workout
findings.text: The Anytime Fitness runner, the Gold's Gym strongman, the CycleBar wheel, and the Row House oars tell you what happens inside before you read the name.

findings.heading: Italics and swooshes add speed
findings.text: 24 Hour Fitness, LA Fitness, UFC Gym, and CycleBar lean or swoosh forward to suggest movement and energy.

findings.heading: Boutique brands are built for apparel
findings.text: SoulCycle, Barry's, Solidcore, and F45 use short, bold names that look good on t-shirts, water bottles, and social media.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a gym logo
checklistItems: Does the logo signal the right price point, from budget to luxury?
Does it read from far away on a building sign or a highway?
Does it work on a key fob, a t-shirt, and an app icon?
Does the symbol or type suggest energy, strength, or calm, depending on the workout?
Will it still work in one colour, embroidered or printed on equipment?

faq.question: What makes a good gym logo?
faq.answer: A good gym logo is bold, simple, and matches the gym's price point and audience. It reads from far away on a sign, works on small items like key fobs and apps, and suggests energy or strength, like the Anytime Fitness runner or the Gold's Gym strongman.

faq.question: What are the most famous gym logos?
faq.answer: The most famous gym logos include Planet Fitness, LA Fitness, Crunch Fitness, 24 Hour Fitness, Anytime Fitness, Gold's Gym, Life Time, Equinox, Orangetheory, and CrossFit.

faq.question: What colours work best for a gym logo?
faq.answer: Budget and mainstream gyms use bright colours like purple, orange, red, and blue to look energetic and friendly. Premium gyms and boutique studios often use black and white to look minimal and exclusive.

faq.question: What fonts do gym logos use?
faq.answer: Most gym logos use bold sans serif or condensed fonts, often in italics to suggest speed. Premium clubs use wide, thin capitals or serifs, and some brands, like David Lloyd and Virgin Active, use a signature script.

faq.question: Should a gym logo have a symbol?
faq.answer: A symbol helps when the logo needs to appear on key fobs, apparel, equipment, and app icons. Many gyms pair a wordmark with a simple icon, like the Planet Fitness PF badge, the 24 Hour Fitness circle, or the CycleBar wheel.
